  "title": "ExeSpec: Verifiable Specification Reasoning for Code LLMs via Execution Grounding",
  "core_problem": "Training-free inference-time methods for LLM code improvement—AlphaCodium (arXiv 2401.08500), CodeT (ICLR 2023), Self-Debugging (arXiv 2304.05128), S* (EMNLP 2025 Findings)—have demonstrated that execution feedback substantially boosts code generation quality using test cases as intermediate representations. Recently, PGS (arXiv 2506.18315, revised May 2026) showed that property-based feedback—abstract behavioral properties rather than I/O test cases—outperforms test-driven methods by 23.1–37.3% relative pass@1 on HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, validating that properties provide richer reasoning scaffolds than point-sample tests. However, three critical limitations remain unresolved. (1) Property reliability: LLM-generated properties are unreliable at scale—PGS reports property generation accuracy of only 48.9% on hard LiveCodeBench problems, ContractEval (arXiv 2510.12047) finds 0% contract satisfaction under standard prompting despite 75–82% pass@1, and CodeSpecBench (arXiv 2604.12268) reveals only 20.2% success at repo-level spec generation—yet no method systematically execution-grounds properties before use to catch hallucinated or internally contradictory specifications. PGS validates properties against public test cases for soundness but does not check inter-property consistency or proactively detect contradictions within the property set. (2) Task generalization: PGS and all property/test-based inference-time methods evaluate exclusively on code generation and simple repair (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), without extension to debugging (where intended-vs-observed behavioral contrasts are needed), issue resolution (where behavioral changes must be extracted from issue context and failing tests), or cross-file completion (where interface contracts must be inferred). NL-Debugging (EMNLP 2025 Main) demonstrated that natural language intermediate representations improve debugging by 4–6pp over code-level methods, but NL descriptions lack the structured, execution-verifiable format needed for systematic property checking. (3) Property decomposition: all property-based methods treat properties as a monolithic category—no work decomposes which property types (preconditions, postconditions, invariants, type constraints, I/O examples) contribute to which task types, preventing targeted optimization. Can execution-grounded, decomposed behavioral specifications address property reliability while extending property-based reasoning across diverse code tasks without model training?",
  "opportunity": "Five research threads converge but remain disconnected: (1) Test-based inference-time refinement (AlphaCodium, CodeT, Self-Debugging, S*, BACE) proves execution feedback improves code generation—AlphaCodium raises CodeContests pass@5 from 19% to 44% on the validation set (12% to 29% on the 165-problem test set), CodeT improves HumanEval pass@1 by +18.8pp via dual execution agreement, S* enables a 3B model to outperform GPT-4o-mini on LiveCodeBench—but all use test cases (point samples) as the intermediate representation. (2) Property-based refinement: PGS (arXiv 2506.18315) demonstrates that LLM-generated abstract properties outperform test-driven feedback by 23.1–37.3% relative pass@1, establishing that property-level reasoning is superior to test-level reasoning for code refinement. However, PGS evaluates only on HumanEval/MBPP/LiveCodeBench (not CodeContests, SWE-bench, or debugging benchmarks), reports property generation accuracy dropping to 48.9% on hard problems, and does not verify inter-property consistency before use. Self-Spec (Agents4Science 2025) showed model-authored specs improve generation by +2–5pp but never verifies specs against execution. ContractEval (arXiv 2510.12047) reveals 0% contract satisfaction under standard prompting despite 75–82% pass@1, rising to only 23–41% with explicit contracts—demonstrating that even when contracts are provided, LLMs struggle to enforce them, motivating execution-based verification. 'From Prompts to Properties' (FSE Companion 2025/LLanMER) finds 30–32% of LLM-generated solutions exhibit partial property failures that pass@k metrics miss entirely. (3) Structured intermediate representations for code: NL-Debugging (EMNLP 2025 Main, arXiv 2505.15356) uses natural language as an intermediate representation for debugging via backtranslation → NL refinement → regeneration, outperforming code-level debugging by 4–6pp on APPS and Codeforces—establishing that higher-level abstractions aid debugging at ExeSpec's target venue. StoryCoder (ACL 2026 Main, arXiv 2604.14631) demonstrates narrative reformulation as structured intermediate reasoning, achieving +18.7% pass@10 across 11 models—concurrent work validating that structured intermediate representations improve code generation. Both use natural language (unverified against execution), not execution-grounded behavioral specifications. (4) Execution-grounded training (Think Like You Execute, RLEF at ICML 2025, FixAudit arXiv 2604.05560) achieves dramatic gains but requires fine-tuning—not usable with frozen models. FixAudit jointly trains fixer and auditor achieving 35–37% improvement on CodeContests, demonstrating the value of audit-style verification but requiring training. (5) Specification quality challenges: CodeSpecBench reveals 20.2% repo-level spec accuracy; 'Revisit Self-Debugging with Self-Generated Tests' (ACL 2025) shows self-generated test feedback introduces systematic bias—motivating richer, verified intermediate representations. The unexploited synthesis: PGS proved properties outperform tests, but property reliability remains the bottleneck (48.9% accuracy on hard problems). Execution grounding can close this gap—verifying LLM-generated property-level specs before use, catching hallucinated and contradictory properties. Additionally, decomposing properties into typed components (pre/postconditions, invariants, type constraints) and evaluating across task types (generation, debugging, issue resolution, completion) addresses the generalization gap that no prior work has tested.",
  "landscape": "**Test-based inference-time methods.** AlphaCodium (arXiv 2401.08500, Jan 2024) is a training-free multi-stage flow with problem reflection, AI test generation, and iterative execution-based refinement with test anchoring, raising CodeContests validation-set pass@5 from 19% to 44% and test-set pass@5 from 12% to 29% with GPT-4. CodeT (ICLR 2023, arXiv 2207.10397) generates tests via LLMs and uses dual execution agreement for solution selection, improving HumanEval pass@1 by +18.8pp. Self-Debugging (arXiv 2304.05128) teaches LLMs to iteratively debug using execution results and natural language explanations, achieving up to 12% improvement on TransCoder and MBPP. 'Revisit Self-Debugging with Self-Generated Tests' (ACL 2025 Long, arXiv 2501.12793) reveals systematic bias in self-generated tests—in-execution debugging using intermediate program states mitigates this, demonstrating that test quality is a fundamental bottleneck for test-based methods. S* (EMNLP 2025 Findings, arXiv 2502.14382) combines parallel sampling with sequential debugging and adaptive distinguishing input synthesis, enabling a 3B model to outperform GPT-4o-mini on LiveCodeBench. BACE (GECCO 2026, arXiv 2603.28653) treats generated tests as noisy sensors via Bayesian updates, outperforming CodeSIM by +2.5–5.4pp on LiveCodeBench v6. All use test cases as the intermediate representation—point samples that verify specific inputs but don't capture universal behavioral properties.

**Property-based and specification approaches.** PGS (arXiv 2506.18315, June 2025; revised as 'Effective LLM Code Refinement via Property-Oriented and Structurally Minimal Feedback', May 2026) is the closest prior work. PGS introduces a Generator-Tester framework where the Tester generates abstract behavioral properties (e.g., 'the product of output factors must equal the input integer') and validates code against them using property-based testing, with structurally minimal counterexamples as feedback. PGS achieves 23.1–37.3% relative pass@1 improvement over TDD methods (Reflexion, Self-Debugging, MGDebugger) using DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Qwen2.5-Coder, and DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-32B on HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench. PGS validates properties against public test cases for soundness, reporting property generation accuracy of 82.4% (easy), 62.8% (medium), and 48.9% (hard) on LiveCodeBench. Critically, PGS does not check inter-property consistency, does not evaluate on CodeContests, SWE-bench, or debugging benchmarks, and treats properties as a monolithic category without decomposing which property types contribute to which tasks. ExeSpec differs from PGS in three ways: (a) execution grounding verifies specs before use via candidate-code probes and cross-spec consistency checks, catching hallucinated and contradictory specs that PGS's public-test validation misses; (b) evaluation spans four task types (generation, debugging, issue resolution, completion) on benchmarks PGS does not cover (CodeContests, SWE-bench Pro, DebugBench); (c) a 5-component schema with controlled ablation decomposes property contributions per task type. Self-Spec (Agents4Science 2025) has LLMs author specification languages before code generation, improving GPT-4o HumanEval pass@1 from 87% to 92%, but only evaluates on HumanEval and never verifies specs against execution. ContractEval (arXiv 2510.12047) benchmarks contract satisfaction in code generation, finding 0% satisfaction under standard prompting despite 75–82% pass@1 scores, 23–41% with explicit contracts, and 49–53% with example-augmented specifications—simultaneously validating that LLMs need external grounding for contract/spec enforcement AND quantifying the difficulty of the spec quality challenge. 'From Prompts to Properties' (FSE Companion 2025/LLanMER) applies property-based testing to evaluate LLM code, finding 30–32% partial property failures that pass@k metrics miss, motivating property-level evaluation. SpecRover/AutoCodeRover-v2 (ICSE 2025) performs iterative NL specification inference for automated program repair, achieving 19.31% on SWE-bench. VibeRepair (arXiv 2602.08263) translates code into NL behavioral specs for repair but specs are imprecise. SSDE (FSE Companion 2026, arXiv 2605.02455) uses Gherkin specifications and domain models for repo-level MVC generation—concurrent work demonstrating structured specs guide LLM generation, but requires human-authored specifications. CodeSpecBench (arXiv 2604.12268) benchmarks LLM spec generation showing only 20.2% repo-level pass rate, motivating execution-based verification.

**Structured intermediate representations.** NL-Debugging (EMNLP 2025 Main, ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-main.80, arXiv 2505.15356) uses natural language as an intermediate representation for code debugging via a three-stage pipeline: backtranslation (buggy code → NL sketch), NL refinement (identify and correct logical flaws in the NL representation using execution feedback), and regeneration (refined NL → corrected code). NL-Debugging outperforms code-level Self-Debugging by 4–6pp pass@1 on APPS and Codeforces across difficulty levels using GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite. The key finding is that the 'Sketch' NL format—detailed natural language descriptions—enables broader modification space than code-level edits, and that refinement in the NL space (not NL→code translation) drives the gains. This establishes structured intermediate representations as valuable for debugging at ExeSpec's target venue (EMNLP). ExeSpec's specifications provide a more structured, execution-verifiable intermediate representation than free-form NL sketches—enabling systematic property checking rather than holistic NL reasoning. StoryCoder (ACL 2026 Main, arXiv 2604.14631) transforms code generation problems into structured narratives (task overview, constraints, test examples), achieving +18.7% zero-shot pass@10 across 11 models on HumanEval, LiveCodeBench, and Codeforces—concurrent training-free work validating structured reformulation, but using narrative structure rather than behavioral specifications. SCoT (ACL 2024) adds program structure to CoT without execution grounding.

**Execution-grounded and RL training methods.** Think Like You Execute (arXiv 2512.00127) achieves +22–27pp on CRUXEval/LiveCodeBench via fine-tuning on 54K execution-trace-verified rationales. EG-CFG (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.10948) uses real-time execution via beam search over candidate lines—computationally expensive and generation-only. RLEF (ICML 2025) trains code LLMs with RL execution feedback. Think Anywhere (arXiv 2603.29957) enables on-demand reasoning during code generation via RL training. CURE (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) co-evolves coder and tester via RL. FixAudit (arXiv 2604.05560) jointly trains a fixer and auditor—the auditor generates new tests revealing implementation-specific bugs in the fixer's candidate code, achieving 35–37% pass@1 improvement on APPS, CodeContests, and xCodeEval with a 7B model. All require training—not applicable with frozen models.

**The gap.** PGS established that property-based feedback outperforms test-based feedback for code generation. Three open questions remain: (1) Can execution grounding improve property reliability beyond PGS's public-test validation (addressing the 48.9% accuracy on hard problems)? (2) Do property-based approaches generalize to debugging, issue resolution, and completion—task types no property-based method has evaluated? (3) Which property types contribute to which tasks? No work addresses all three questions in a unified, training-free framework with controlled experimental design.",
  "approach": "We propose ExeSpec, a training-free inference-time framework that uses execution-grounded behavioral specifications as verifiable structured intermediate reasoning for LLM code tasks. Building on PGS's demonstration that property-based feedback outperforms test-based feedback for code generation, ExeSpec advances the property-based paradigm in three directions: (1) execution grounding that verifies spec consistency and catches hallucinated properties before downstream use, (2) extension to debugging, issue resolution, and cross-file completion beyond generation/repair, and (3) decomposition of specifications into typed components with controlled ablation.

**Stage 1: Spec Elicitation.** Given a task input, prompt the LLM to generate structured behavioral specifications in a lightweight JSON schema containing five component types: (a) I/O example pairs (shared with both PGS properties and AlphaCodium test cases—the overlap region), (b) preconditions (constraints on valid inputs/states, e.g., 'n >= 0', 'input list is non-empty'), (c) postconditions (properties guaranteed on outputs, e.g., 'output is sorted in ascending order', 'len(output) == len(input)'), (d) type constraints (parameter and return type annotations with generics), and (e) invariants (loop invariants, monotonicity, ordering properties). The schema is task-adapted: generation tasks derive specs from docstrings; debugging tasks elicit intended-vs-observed behavioral contrasts; issue resolution tasks extract expected behavioral changes from issue descriptions and failing test context; completion tasks infer interface contracts from cross-file context.

**Stage 2: Execution Grounding.** This is ExeSpec's primary differentiator from PGS. While PGS validates properties against public test cases for soundness, ExeSpec additionally performs: (i) cross-spec consistency checking—verifying that preconditions, postconditions, invariants, and type constraints are mutually satisfiable and non-contradictory (e.g., a postcondition asserting 'output is sorted' does not contradict an invariant asserting 'elements maintain original order'); (ii) candidate-code probing—generating a quick candidate solution, executing against spec-derived assertions including both I/O examples AND postcondition property checks, identifying spec-execution mismatches, and revising contradicted specs before final generation. For debugging tasks: execute the buggy code, compare execution traces against specs to identify precisely which behavioral constraints are violated, producing structured violation reports. For issue resolution (SWE-bench Pro): extract behavioral expectations from issue descriptions and failing tests, generate specs characterizing the intended fix behavior, and validate spec consistency against the existing test suite via Docker-based execution. For cross-file completion: static grounding via type inference from imported modules, parameter/return types from call-site usage context, and validation via type checkers (mypy/pyright for Python, tsc for TypeScript). When full execution is unavailable, static grounding serves as fallback: cross-spec consistency checking, type inference, and contradiction detection.

**Stage 3: Spec-Guided Task Completion.** Feed grounded specs alongside the original task input to the LLM for final output. When outputs violate specs, structured violation reports (which constraints failed, expected vs. actual, which spec component) feed back for iterative refinement (up to 3 rounds). Unlike PGS's structurally minimal counterexamples, ExeSpec's feedback references typed behavioral properties ('postcondition: output must be monotonically increasing') with component attribution, enabling the LLM to reason about which aspect of behavioral intent was violated.

**Baselines and controlled experiments.** The experimental design isolates contributions through six controlled conditions: (a) ExeSpec full (5-component specs + execution grounding), (b) PGS baseline (property-based testing following PGS's Generator-Tester framework, reimplemented on our benchmarks—the paper's critical comparison, isolating the contribution of execution grounding and component decomposition beyond PGS's approach), (c) AlphaCodium-style baseline (problem reflection + AI test generation + iterative execution/refinement with test anchoring—isolating the property-vs-test distinction, extending PGS's finding to new benchmarks), (d) Self-Spec baseline (specs without execution grounding—isolating the grounding contribution), (e) direct prompting (no intermediate reasoning), (f) NL-Debugging baseline on DebugBench only (NL intermediate representation via backtranslation/refinement/regeneration—isolating structured specs vs. free-form NL for debugging, providing venue-relevant comparison to EMNLP 2025 work). The delta between (a) and (b) is the paper's core contribution—whether execution grounding and component decomposition provide gains beyond PGS's property-based approach. The delta between (b) and (c) replicates PGS's finding (properties > tests) on new benchmarks (CodeContests, DebugBench, SWE-bench Pro) where PGS has not been evaluated. A critical spec-component ablation further decomposes: (i) full specs (I/O + pre/postconditions + invariants + type constraints), (ii) I/O-only specs (functionally equivalent to test cases—if this matches full specs, the novelty claim collapses), (iii) structural specs only (pre/postconditions + invariants + type constraints, no I/O)—this ablation is the critical honesty test.

**Benchmarks.** Primary benchmarks with all six conditions + spec-component ablation: DebugBench (C++/Java/Python debugging—specs naturally capture intended-vs-observed behavioral contrasts, and NL-Debugging comparison is venue-relevant), CodeContests (competitive programming—direct comparison to AlphaCodium on its home benchmark, and first evaluation of PGS-style property feedback on CodeContests), and SWE-bench Pro (real-world issue resolution—adopted as co-primary benchmark given that SWE-bench Verified is compromised by contamination in frontier models; OpenAI stopped reporting Verified scores in February 2026 after finding frontier models could reproduce verbatim gold patches. We use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/32B, sub-frontier models unlikely to exhibit the verbatim gold-patch reproduction observed in GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.5, providing a contamination-resistant evaluation baseline. We report results on both SWE-bench Pro and Verified for completeness, noting the community's shift toward Pro for reliable evaluation). Supplementary benchmarks with ExeSpec vs. direct prompting only: HumanEval+/MBPP+ (for Self-Spec and PGS comparability—PGS reports results on these benchmarks, enabling direct numerical comparison), CrossCodeEval and RepoBench (cross-file completion with static grounding via type checkers). We explicitly acknowledge that cross-file completion relies on weaker static grounding than dynamic execution and report the proportion of instances where only static grounding was available.

**Models.** We use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct as established dense models with strong code performance and reproducible vLLM inference; the method is model-agnostic and we expect gains to transfer to newer architectures including MoE models (e.g., Qwen3-Coder-Next). Using established models enables direct comparison with PGS, which evaluates Qwen2.5-Coder on the same model family.

**Analysis.** Beyond standard metrics: (1) spec quality analysis—correlation between spec correctness and downstream task performance; (2) grounding effectiveness—proportion of hallucinated specs caught by execution grounding vs. PGS's public-test validation (the key comparison); (3) spec-component contribution—which spec types most improve each task type; (4) test overfitting rates—proportion of solutions passing visible tests but failing held-out tests, comparing ExeSpec vs. baselines; (5) property accuracy by difficulty—replicating PGS's accuracy breakdown (82.4%/62.8%/48.9% by difficulty) on our benchmarks and measuring whether execution grounding improves it; (6) qualitative case studies showing where execution-grounded specs enable corrections that both test-only and ungrounded property methods miss.",

Issues: ["CRITICAL — PGS v2 FACTUAL ERRORS PERSIST FROM ROUND 8 (6TH ROUND RAISING THIS ISSUE): The idea states 'PGS achieves 23.1–37.3% relative pass@1 improvement... on HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench' and 'PGS does not evaluate on CodeContests, SWE-bench, or debugging benchmarks.' PGS v2 (May 1, 2026) evaluates on FIVE benchmarks: HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, AND SWE-bench Verified.
